title: Identity theft: recovery, freezes and disputes
body_md:
## A copy of your ID is not yet a signature

The letter says your name and ID number were in a file that leaked. Your balance is where it should be and nobody has phoned. Somewhere a stranger holds a copy of your details, and so far nobody has signed anything with them. Your first job is to find out which of the two you are dealing with: what was exposed, and what was actually used. A breach notice can justify protective steps before any misuse. An account you never opened, a debt notice, a tax filing or a benefit claim in your name is another matter. Each is a separate dispute with the organization involved, so keep a record of every case and how it ends. Misuse of your tax record, your benefits or your medical insurance goes to that agency or insurer. A credit freeze won’t repair it.

### US: a freeze, a report, and the disputes

In the US, a free security freeze at **each** of Equifax, Experian and TransUnion stops lenders from pulling your credit report when someone applies for new credit. It does not stop anyone using your existing accounts, it does not cover every other kind of identity misuse, and it does not reach lenders outside that system. You can lift it for a legitimate application. A fraud alert is milder: it asks lenders to verify who you are but leaves your report open to them, and an initial alert placed at one bureau is passed on to the others. Once misuse has happened, the FTC’s IdentityTheft.gov builds a tailored report and recovery plan. Then read your credit reports, contact the issuer of every account you did not open, and dispute wrong entries with the bureau and with the business that supplied them. Keep every written confirmation. A police report can help in a particular process, but it is not required everywhere.

### Don’t export the US rules

The UK, the EU, the UAE and other systems don’t all work like the American three-bureau freeze. Look up the local bureau, lender and identity-authority procedures. In Russia, the Bank of Russia describes a **self-ban on certain consumer loans**, which you can set through Gosuslugi or an MFC. It excludes, among others, mortgages and some secured and education loans. It is not the same as a US freeze, and it does not block spending on an existing credit card. Check its current status and terms in the official service.

### What a freeze can’t undo, and how to lift it

If someone has used your existing card or bank account, tell that institution at once; an identity measure cannot undo the transaction. If you are making a genuine credit application in the US, ask the lender which bureau it uses and arrange a temporary lift of that bureau’s freeze through the official channel. In Russia, if your planned consumer loan falls under a self-ban, apply to cancel it through Gosuslugi or an MFC and allow for the cooling interval: cancellation takes effect on the second calendar day after its record enters your credit history. Confirm the status before you apply. Mortgages are outside the Russian self-ban, so ask the lender about a mortgage delay instead of blaming the ban. Be wary of paid “identity repair” services that promise a guaranteed result. Recovery ends when each fraudulent record has been resolved and the protections you chose are written down, not after a set number of months.

widget_config.goal: Tell exposure from misuse, and use the protective and dispute process that fits where you live, without assuming a US freeze works everywhere.
widget_config.today_action: In the US, find the official freeze pages of all three bureaus. Elsewhere, find out where you check your credit file and how you dispute an entry with a lender. Don’t type any personal data into this lesson.
widget_config.scope: The US freeze and FTC procedures and the Russian consumer-loan self-ban each apply only in their own country; anywhere else, check locally. The people and events in the examples are invented.

blocks.title: A breach, then a stranger’s card
blocks.situation: On Monday a US shopper gets a breach notice from a retailer she has bought from. By Friday her credit report lists a store card she never opened.
blocks.analysis: She freezes her file at each US bureau to cut the risk of new credit, reports the misuse at IdentityTheft.gov, contacts the card issuer and disputes the entry on her report. The freeze does nothing about the card that is already open. That account needs a dispute of its own.

blocks.title: A mortgage held up by your own freeze
blocks.situation: Omar froze his US credit reports months ago. Now a mortgage lender tells him it cannot pull a report for his application.
blocks.analysis: The freeze is doing its job, and nothing here points to new fraud. Omar confirms the lender through a channel he already knows, learns which bureau it uses, lifts that bureau’s freeze for a while and puts it back afterwards.

blocks.title: A credit report entry you don’t know
blocks.setup: An invented case set in the US. Your credit report lists a store card you don’t recognize, and an email advertises a paid “instant identity repair.” Each decision is a separate US snapshot, and no step assumes you took an earlier action.

steps.prompt: You want to stop anyone opening new credit in your name. What do you do?

choices.text: Place free freezes with all three US nationwide bureaus.
choices.consequence: Lenders can no longer pull those reports for new credit.
choices.explanation: A freeze at one bureau does not automatically cover the other two.

choices.consequence: New applications can keep going through.
choices.explanation: A paid promise is not a protective control.

steps.prompt: New snapshot: a store card you never opened is already on your report. How do you deal with that account?

choices.text: Assume the freeze wipes it out.
choices.consequence: The fraudulent account stays on your file.
choices.explanation: Preventing new accounts and correcting old ones are different jobs.

choices.text: Dispute it with the issuer and the relevant bureau, using the FTC recovery plan if it fits.
choices.consequence: That record gets a challenge of its own.
choices.explanation: A freeze alone does not delete existing entries.

steps.prompt: New snapshot: an issuer you reached through its official channel asks for a report or case reference for a new dispute. What do you give?

choices.text: A verified report or case reference if you have one; if not, say so and ask what the issuer needs.
choices.consequence: The issuer gets an accurate reference, or explains how to obtain the record it requires.
choices.explanation: Don’t invent a case number, and don’t send documents through an ad’s upload link.

choices.text: Your whole identity file, uploaded through the repair ad’s link.
choices.consequence: Even more of your sensitive data is now out of your hands.
choices.explanation: An ad does not prove who is asking, and it is not the issuer.

steps.prompt: New US snapshot: a genuine loan application is due next month, and your credit freeze is active. What now?

choices.text: Remove all freezes for good, since applications are impossible otherwise.
choices.consequence: You lose protection you did not need to lose.

choices.text: Plan a temporary lift at the bureau the lender uses, then restore the freeze.
choices.consequence: The lender’s check goes through and the protection comes back.
choices.explanation: Lift only the bureau the lender uses, and confirm the lender independently first.

blocks.debrief: A US freeze limits some new credit; disputes repair the records that already exist. Other countries work differently. Replay the choices you did not take, and keep real identity details out of the practice.

questions.prompt: Does a US credit freeze stop fraud on a card you already have?

choices.explanation: A freeze limits access to your reports for new credit. It does not touch an existing card.

choices.text: No. Report misuse of the existing card to its issuer separately.

questions.prompt: A Russian resident is weighing a consumer-loan self-ban. Which limit matters?

choices.text: It does not cover every credit product, or use of an existing card.
choices.explanation: The Bank of Russia lists the exclusions and the existing-card limit.

choices.text: It is identical to a US three-bureau freeze.
choices.explanation: The mechanism and the scope differ.

questions.prompt: Your own US mortgage lender cannot pull a report. What should you do?

choices.text: Verify the lender and temporarily lift the relevant freeze.
choices.explanation: The genuine application goes ahead without giving up protection for good.

choices.text: Treat every failed pull as proof of identity theft.
choices.explanation: Your own freeze can explain it.
